headline: Claims the metric Blaschke conjecture: injectivity radius equal to diameter forces a round sphere or projective space.
scope: Connected closed smooth Riemannian manifolds of positive dimension whose global injectivity radius equals their diameter.
plain: On a round sphere, every straightest path stays shortest until it reaches the opposite point. A few other symmetric spaces, the projective spaces and the Cayley plane, share this property. The metric Blaschke conjecture says no other closed smooth space has it. Surfaces and some other cases were settled earlier. This paper claims the full classification in every dimension.
doesNot: This does not cover spaces that are not smooth or not closed. It has no Lean check.
origin: This result comes from an unreleased OpenAI model, published in the openai/math release on 6 October 2026.

scorecard.firstStepBy: Wilhelm Blaschke, who asked the original question for surfaces
scorecard.significanceWhy: It claims a long-standing conjecture in Riemannian geometry, studied for about a century, in every dimension.

explanation:
Take a round sphere of radius 1. The farthest two points can be is π, half a great circle, so the diameter is π. Start at the north pole and walk along any straight path. It stays the shortest route until it hits the south pole, at distance exactly π. So every straightest path from every point stays shortest for exactly the diameter. Now glue each point of the sphere to its opposite point. This gives the real projective plane. Its diameter is π/2, and its closed straightest paths have length π, twice the diameter. Again every straightest path stays shortest for exactly the diameter. A flat square torus with side 1 is different. Some straight paths stop being shortest after length 1/2. But its diameter is the half-diagonal, √2/2, about 0.707. The two numbers differ.

The injectivity radius at a point is how far you can go in every direction before straight paths stop being unique. The smallest value over all points is the global injectivity radius. It is never larger than the diameter. A Blaschke manifold is one where the two are equal[2]. The round spheres, the real, complex and quaternionic projective spaces, and the Cayley plane are all Blaschke. These are the compact rank-one symmetric spaces, the most symmetric curved spaces of their kind. The metric Blaschke conjecture asks whether they are the only ones[3].

Green settled the surface case[4]. Berger, Kazdan, Weinstein and Yang settled the sphere and real projective cases[5]. Yang showed a Blaschke manifold shaped like complex projective space has the model's volume[6]. The paper claims the full result. Every Blaschke manifold is, up to scale, one of these symmetric spaces[1].

The plan has two volume bounds. First, the paper claims every Blaschke manifold has at least the volume of its model at the same diameter[7]. Equality holds only for the model itself[8]. So it is enough to prove the volume is at most the model's[9]. The lower bound uses Jacobi fields, which measure how nearby straight paths spread apart. For the quaternionic spaces, the upper bound was the main obstacle. The paper proves it with topology, using characteristic classes and the space of all closed straight paths[10].

How sure is this? There is no Lean check. A computer proof checker has not looked at any part of it. The proof combines delicate analysis with algebraic topology. No specialist review of the paper has been published.
hypeCheck: Landmark-level claim if the proof holds: it would settle the metric Blaschke conjecture in every dimension. The proof is long and has no Lean check or published specialist review.
